hazards.defend-every-point: You argued back against every point of feedback. Listening first, asking a question to understand and thanking the person, even if you disagree, gets you far more from feedback than defending yourself does.
hazards.feedback-about-the-person: You said your teammate was just bad at it. Feedback about the person hurts and gives them nothing to work on; feedback about the work, what they did and what might help, is specific, kind and useful.
hazards.one-voice-decides: You let the loudest voice decide for the whole team. Good teams hear from everyone, especially the quiet members, before deciding; the loudest idea is not always the best one.
hazards.wet-floor-sprint: You ran across a wet patch of court to reach the huddle. Wet sports floors are slippery; you walk round the cone, and the coach has the floor dried before anyone plays on it.

interrupts.alert: One teammate has gone quiet and moved to the edge of the group while others talk over them.
interrupts.cue: Invite them back in and ask for their idea.
interrupts.missNote: Nobody noticed, and the teammate sat out the rest of the session.
interrupts.why: Being left out is painful and it loses the team a voice. Inviting them back and asking for their idea shows the team values everyone, and it is often exactly the idea the group needed.
interrupts.wrongNote: That leaves them out. Invite them in. Choose the response that deals with it now.

interrupts.alert: The team coach asks you to give feedback to a teammate on the drill they just led.
interrupts.cue: Say something specific they did well and one thing to try next.
interrupts.missNote: You said it was fine, and your teammate had nothing to work on.
interrupts.why: The coach is checking you can put the feedback steps into practice on the spot. Being specific and kind shows you can help a teammate improve without knocking their confidence.
interrupts.wrongNote: That is too vague to help. Choose the response that deals with it now.

lateNotes.ktf-checkin: The check-in comes at the very end of the session.
lateNotes.ktf-team-log: The team review is written once the session is done — nothing to record yet.

name: Teamwork and Feedback

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Mark the three things on the team board that help a team work together.

decoyNotes.ktf-trophy: A reminder of past success, but it does not make this team work.

itemNotes.ktf-goal: Everyone pulling towards the same thing.

steps.prompt: Mark the three things on the team board that help a team work together.
steps.title: Find what makes a team work
steps.why: Teams work well when everyone knows the shared goal, each person has a clear role, and there are agreed ways to talk, like taking turns and listening. Finding those three on the team board shows that good teamwork is built on purpose, not left to luck.

steps.cue: Read the coach's card: walk round the cone, never across a wet court.
steps.prompt: Read the coach's card: walk round the cone, never across a wet court.
steps.title: Walk round the wet patch
steps.why: A wet patch on a sports floor is as slippery as ice. Walking round the cone and letting the coach dry it is the rule every team follows, because an injured teammate helps nobody, and looking after each other is where teamwork starts. A wet patch is also a test of the team: the one who stops to warn others is doing the team's work.

steps.cue: Ask if they want feedback, name something specific, suggest one next step, then listen.

itemNames.ktf-ord-specific: 2 · name something specific that went well

steps.outOfOrderNote: Out of order. Ask if they want feedback before you give it.
steps.prompt: Ask if they want feedback, name something specific, suggest one next step, then listen.
steps.title: Put the feedback steps in order
steps.why: Asking first makes feedback something offered, not forced. Naming something specific that went well, suggesting one clear next step and then listening to their reply keeps feedback useful and kind, and it is the pattern good coaches use every day. Skipping the listening step turns feedback into a lecture, and people stop hearing lectures quickly.

steps.cue: Stay quiet and listen fully until your teammate has finished.
steps.holdBreakNote: You jumped in before they finished. Let them finish, then reply.
steps.prompt: Stay quiet and listen fully until your teammate has finished.
steps.title: Hold your reply while a teammate speaks
steps.why: Waiting until someone has finished, instead of planning your answer while they talk, is what listening really means. It shows respect, it means you hear the whole idea, and it often changes what you were going to say. People can tell when they are really being listened to, and it makes them more willing to listen back.

steps.cue: Turn the role wheel so each teammate gets a different job this round.
steps.prompt: Turn the role wheel so each teammate gets a different job this round.
steps.title: Turn the role wheel to share the jobs
steps.why: Rotating roles lets everyone try leading, recording and checking, and stops the same people always doing the same jobs. It builds skills across the team and shows everyone what each role takes.

steps.cue: Commit when the tone meter shows your feedback is specific and kind.

gauge.label: TONE
gauge.missNote: Not in the band. Make it more specific, or kinder.

steps.prompt: Commit when the tone meter shows your feedback is specific and kind.
steps.title: Judge the tone of your feedback
steps.why: Feedback that is too vague helps nobody, and feedback that is harsh makes people stop listening. Aiming for specific and kind, the middle of the band, gives your teammate something clear to work on and the confidence to try it. The same words can land as help or as criticism depending on how they are said, so tone matters.

steps.cue: Drag the specific, kind feedback card to your teammate's spot.

drag.missNote: Not given yet. Take the specific, kind card to your teammate.

steps.prompt: Drag the specific, kind feedback card to your teammate's spot.
steps.title: Choose a helpful feedback card
steps.why: A card that says what went well and one thing to try next gives your teammate a clear way forward. Choosing it over a vague or harsh card is practising exactly the words that make feedback land well.

steps.cue: Say what you do when someone gives you feedback, even if you disagree.
steps.prompt: Say what you do when someone gives you feedback, even if you disagree.
steps.title: Say how to receive feedback well
steps.why: Receiving feedback well means listening, asking a question to understand and thanking the person, then deciding what to use. Saying that aloud builds the habit, and it is one of the most valuable skills in school, sport and work. Nobody has to agree with every piece of feedback, but hearing it fully before deciding is fair to both people.

steps.cue: Look at the practice team talk and mark each problem.

decoyNotes.ktf-tt-thanks: Thanking teammates is good practice. Keep it.

itemNames.ktf-tt-person: feedback about the person, not the work

steps.prompt: Look at the practice team talk and mark each problem.
steps.title: Spot the problems in a practice team talk
steps.why: Team talks go wrong in familiar ways: feedback aimed at the person, a quiet teammate never asked and a decision made by the loudest voice. Spotting them in a practice talk helps you notice and fix them in real ones.

steps.cue: Keep the discussion's temperature in the calm band as teammates disagree.
steps.holdBreakNote: The discussion got heated. Slow down, name what you agree on, and bring it back.
steps.prompt: Keep the discussion's temperature in the calm band as teammates disagree.
steps.title: Keep a disagreement calm
steps.why: Disagreements are normal and can make a team's ideas better, as long as they stay calm and about the ideas. Keeping your voice steady, naming what you agree on and looking for a fair way to decide keeps the team together. When a discussion stays calm, the team can use the disagreement to find a better plan than either side started with.

steps.cue: Write what the team did well, one thing to improve and who will do what.
steps.prompt: Write what the team did well, one thing to improve and who will do what.
steps.title: Record the team's review
steps.why: A short team review turns one session into learning for the next. Writing a strength, one improvement and clear actions means everyone leaves knowing what comes next.

steps.cue: Thank one teammate for a specific thing they did today.
steps.prompt: Thank one teammate for a specific thing they did today.
steps.title: Thank a teammate for something specific
steps.why: Specific thanks tells someone exactly what they did that helped, which makes them more likely to do it again. It ends a session warmly and builds the trust that good teams rely on.

steps.cue: How did working as a team feel today? What would you do differently?
steps.prompt: How did working as a team feel today? What would you do differently?
steps.title: Check in at the end of the session
steps.why: A check-in lets every learner say how teamwork felt for them, which may be different for quiet and loud members, and helps the coach and teacher support everyone. It is not marked, and a trusted adult is always there to talk to. Some people find group work easy and others find it tiring, and both are normal things to say out loud.

supportLine: your teacher, a school counsellor or a trusted adult at home — if anything in this lesson was hard, talk it through afterwards
tagline: Specific, kind and useful — give feedback on the work, never the person
